hints: Focus on how $\text{NH}_4^+$ is formed from ammonia, and whether it would accept or donate a proton in water.
Recall that ammonia is pyramidal, but adding a fourth $\text{H}^+$ uses up the lone pair, so count the bond pairs and lone pairs now on nitrogen.
Think about what happens once a dative bond is formed, and whether you can still tell it apart from the other three covalent bonds.
walkthrough:
**Start From How Ammonium Forms**

Think of ammonium as ammonia that has picked up an extra proton. Ammonia has a lone pair, so it acts as a base.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$$

**Check Acid-Base Behaviour**

Because $\text{NH}_4^+$ is made by gaining a proton, the reverse reaction must be losing a proton. That makes it a Bronsted-Lowry acid, not a base.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$$

**Check Shape and Bond Angle**

In $\text{NH}_3$ there are 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, so pyramidal with about $107^\circ$. In $\text{NH}_4^+$ the lone pair is now used to bond the fourth H, so there are 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs.

VSEPR rule:
$$\text{4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs = tetrahedral, } 109.5^\circ$$

**Check Are The Four Bonds Identical?**

Three N-H bonds were originally covalent and one was dative from N to $\text{H}^+$. Once formed, the electrons are shared equally and spread out tetrahedrally. You cannot distinguish them, so all four N-H bonds are identical in length and strength.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{NH}_4^+$ in water donates a proton to water to form $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so it is a weak Bronsted-Lowry acid. It is $\text{NH}_3$ that is the weak base, students often mix the conjugate pair around.
options.B: Incorrect. Ammonia gas is released when an ammonium salt reacts with a base like NaOH, not with an acid like HCl. Adding dilute HCl just provides $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{H}^+$, with no reaction to give $\text{NH}_3$.
options.C: Incorrect. Pyramidal with $107^\circ$ describes ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, which has a lone pair. Ammonium, $\text{NH}_4^+$, has four bonding pairs and no lone pair, so it is tetrahedral with $109.5^\circ$.
options.D: Correct. Although one N-H bond starts as a dative (coordinate) bond from nitrogen to $\text{H}^+$, once formed all four bonds are equivalent. The positive charge is spread over the whole ion and the tetrahedral arrangement makes them identical.
